query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism expected to operate across the test regime, predicts performance relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, specifies relevant temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: If the CoCrFeNi matrix is doped with a moderate amount of Mo (e.g., 5–10 at.%) using vacuum arc melting, then a continuous Mo-rich tribo-oxide layer will form under sliding from room temperature up to 800 °C in air, reducing both friction and wear relative to undoped CoCrFeNi.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast or homogenized single-phase CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy matrix without Mo.
generation.intervention: Add Mo via vacuum arc melting to form a CoCrFeNiMo alloy with approximately 5–10 at.% Mo.
generation.conditions: Conduct pin-on-disk (or ball-on-disk) sliding tests in air from 25 to 800 °C under moderate normal loads (10–30 N) and typical linear sliding speeds (0.1–0.5 m/s).
generation.structural_mediator: In situ formation of a Mo-containing oxide tribofilm and possible Mo-rich phases in the FCC matrix, enhancing tribological performance across the full temperature range.
generation.mechanism: Mo accelerates the creation of lubricious and protective oxides that limit adhesive and abrasive contact at high temperature while bolstering load-bearing capacity in the base alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to undoped CoCrFeNi, the Mo-doped alloy will exhibit a 30–50% lower coefficient of friction and at least an order-of-magnitude decrease in wear rate under the same test parameters from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.baseline: Untreated CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy tested under identical conditions without added Mo.
generation.boundary: The effect is most assured in air environments under moderate loads up to 800 °C; in oxygen-deficient or extremely high-load conditions, the benefit may be reduced.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal Mo content for uniform tribo-oxide formation and its compatibility with other minor elements remain unclear, necessitating further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a set of CoCrFeNi alloys with varying levels of Mo (0, 5, and 10 at.%) via vacuum arc melting, followed by consistent homogenization. Perform pin-on-disk tests in air from 25 °C to 800 °C at fixed loads and speeds, tracking friction and wear using both in situ measurements and post-test surface analysis.
measurements: Steady-state coefficient of friction across test durations
Specific wear rate (using volume loss per N·m via standard Archard analysis)
Microstructural characterization of tribofilms using SEM, EDS, or XPS
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Mo-containing alloys do not form a persistent Mo-rich oxide film and show no improvement in friction and wear relative to the undoped CoCrFeNi across the tested temperatures, then the hypothesis is refuted.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractAlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy (HEA) films with strong amorphization were obtained by co-filter cathode vacuum arc deposition, and the effect of thermal shock on the films was investigated in order to explore the protection mechanism of HEA films against mechanical components in extreme service environments. The results show that after annealing at 800 °C for 1 h, the formation of a dense ZrTiO4 composite oxide layer on the surface actively prevents the oxidation from continuing, so that the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film exhibits excellent oxidation resistance at 800 °C in air. In the friction-corrosion coupling environment, the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film annealed at 800 °C for 1 h shows the best tribocorrosion resistance due to the stable dense microstructure and excellent mechanical properties, and its ΔOCP, COF and wear rate possess the smallest values of 0.055, 0.04 and 1.34 × 10−6 mm−3·N−1·m−1.Keywords: AlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy film, thermal shock, oxidation, tribocorrosion

To further investigate the friction and wear mechanism of CoCrFeNiMo HEA coatings, an EDS mapping was conducted on the oxide layer formed after the coating’s friction and wear test. From Figure 13a, it is clearly observed that the black areas are oxide formations, primarily iron oxides, which some studies [,] suggest are γ-Fe2O3. The gray areas are enriched with Mo elements, which are presumed to be the σ-phase. During the process of resisting friction and wear, the ductile FCC phase both stabilizes the hard σ-phase to prevent large-scale grain loss and forms an oxide layer that reduces the wear rate. Meanwhile, the σ-phase, due to its extremely high hardness, limits the generation and propagation of cracks in the FCC phase.
